title: Route-level A/B testing - architecture review (policy precedence + exposure logging)
topics: Routing policy precedence (experiments vs canaries vs fallbacks)
Telemetry pipeline changes and cardinality guardrails
Cost attribution by variant and reporting dataset shape
summary: Internal architecture review for route-level A/B testing. Team aligned on precedence rules and key constraints: (1) experiments should be evaluated at the route level before per-variant fallbacks, but reliability/fail-closed behavior must be preserved; (2) exposure logs must be privacy-safe (no raw PII), sampled, and low-cardinality; (3) telemetry changes need a schema version and strict tag allowlist to avoid blowing up metrics; (4) deterministic assignment needs a documented hash input order with a stable fallback when certain headers aren’t present; (5) streaming reconnect/retry must not change the variant. Open questions were captured for ADR-0187/0188 and metrics schema v1.
questions: If an experiment is configured on a route that also has a canary rollout active, do we disallow it in validation, or define a deterministic precedence rule and allow both?
What is the minimum required stickiness key set for Hosted vs Dedicated (api_key_id always available, but do we support customer-provided user_id header)?
Do we emit exposure at request start, on first token, or at completion (and how do we handle streaming disconnects)?
Do we need a separate ‘assignment’ event and ‘exposure’ event, or can we treat them as the same with an ‘exposure_reason’ field?
What retention window do we need for raw exposure logs vs aggregated metrics to support audits and customer reporting?
action_items: Jordan Lee - Write up the final precedence proposal (experiment vs canary vs fallback) with concrete examples and failure-mode table for ADR-0187 - Due 2026-02-20
Logan Wright - Draft exposure event schema v1 fields + tag allowlist + sampling guidance for ADR-0188 / metrics schema doc - Due 2026-02-21
Nadia Rahman - Confirm cost attribution requirements (token + GPU) and which dimensions can be added without breaking billing/meters - Due 2026-02-21
Mina Haddad - Validate retry/streaming reconnect behavior in gateway and propose how we persist assignment across reconnect - Due 2026-02-24
Marcus Lin - Security pass on hash inputs and any potential PII leakage (esp. customer-provided headers) + access control for exposure logs - Due 2026-02-24
Sean Gallagher - Provide initial guardrail thresholds and alert routing expectations for beta enablement checklist - Due 2026-02-25
Mei Lin - Propose aggregated dataset layout (materialized views) needed by Console results queries (per-variant time series + breakdowns) - Due 2026-02-26
next_steps: Jada + Jordan to update ADR drafts (0187/0188) and circulate for sign-off (Routing, Telemetry, Security, SRE).
Telemetry team to implement exposure ingest behind a feature flag and run a cardinality load test in staging.
Console team to implement validation warnings for overlapping rollouts once precedence is finalized.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up to close open questions (especially stickiness keys + retention).
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Route-level A/B testing - architecture review (policy precedence + exposure logging)
Date: 2026-02-17
Time: 09:00 AM PT
Duration: 58 min
Attendees: Dylan Brooks, Jada Williams, Jordan Lee, Mina Haddad, Ravi Menon, Ethan Park, Logan Wright, Nadia Rahman, Caleb Johnson, Mei Lin, Allison Grant, Sean Gallagher, Marcus Lin, Olivia Grant, Sana Farid, Paula Mendes


[00:00] Dylan Brooks: Alright, cool, I think we’re all on. This is the arch review for route-level A/B testing. We wanna close on precedence, exposure logging, and the telemetry pipeline changes. Goal is to feed the ADRs—0187 and 0188—and unblock the PRD scope.

[00:18] Paula Mendes: And just to anchor, v1 is route-level splits in Console, deterministic assignment, p50/p95/p99, TTFT, cost, error rates, plus optional offline eval suite attachment. No bandits.

[00:30] Jada Williams: Yep. So biggest open question is: where in the routing stack do we evaluate the experiment? Today we have canary rollouts and also fallback policies. We cannot end up with like a double-randomization.

[00:45] Ravi Menon: Right, and we should be explicit: routing is policy engine -> pick target model/config -> then runtime/gateway does the actual proxying. There’s also “fallback” which can be triggered by capacity, timeouts, 5xx, etc.

[01:01] Jordan Lee: The proposed mental model: experiment is a route-level policy that returns a “variant” which maps to a target config. Then *within* that variant request we still allow reliability fallbacks, but we should preserve the variant label for measurement.

[01:17] Mina Haddad: That’s the tricky part. If variant B targets model X and we fallback to model Y because X is out of capacity, do we still call that “variant B”? From measurement it looks like B had bad latency, but actually it was fallback.

[01:33] Logan Wright: From analytics, we can handle that if the events include both the assigned variant and the final served model. But we must be careful with cardinality, like model version strings and routing reason codes.

[01:49] Allison Grant: Yeah, if you add “fallback_reason” with free-form values, Grafana explodes. We need an enum, and it can’t include like request ids or the full model digest.

[02:02] Dylan Brooks: Let’s focus on precedence first. Ravi, can you outline the options?

[02:08] Ravi Menon: Sure. Option A: Experiment evaluated first. It picks variant A/B, then variant config can include canary rules or whatever. But that gets weird, because canary is also a split.

[02:21] Ravi Menon: Option B: Canary evaluated first, then within each canary bucket you do experiment. That’s basically layering splits which can make reporting hard and assignment non-intuitive.

[02:32] Ravi Menon: Option C: We declare experiments and canaries mutually exclusive on the same route. Validation blocks it. That’s simplest, but you lose power users.

[02:41] Paula Mendes: Product-wise, I’m leaning Option C for v1. Most customers will be confused if they have “rollout split” plus “experiment split.”

[02:53] Jada Williams: I agree for v1, but we need a deterministic rule anyway for internal use and for the edge case where someone accidentally overlaps. Validation can catch most, but there will be drift.

[03:08] Jordan Lee: ADR needs an explicit precedence order even if we block. For example: If experiment exists and is active, it overrides canary for that route. Or the opposite.

[03:19] Mina Haddad: From routing correctness: canary is also a “safe rollout” primitive. A/B is measurement. I’d rather canary take precedence for safety. But then customers expect their experiment to run and it won’t.

[03:34] Sean Gallagher: SRE viewpoint: safest is “one traffic shaper per route.” If both are on, that’s an operational footgun. If we must pick, I’d rather degrade to a known safe default—probably the pinned model, not the experiment.

[03:49] Dylan Brooks: So: validate to prevent overlap; on conflict, pick the pinned or stable config? Jordan, can you propose a conflict resolution table?

[04:00] Jordan Lee: Yep. For ADR-0187 we can define: evaluation order is (1) hard blocks like kill switches; (2) entitlement/tier gates; (3) experiment policy if active; (4) canary policy if active; (5) pinned model; (6) default.

[04:17] Mina Haddad: That would make experiment override canary, which I’m not sure about.

[04:23] Ravi Menon: Another take: canary is *also* an experiment, but with guardrails and progressive delivery semantics. If both exist, maybe canary is “higher priority.” But then reporting in Console says “experiment running” while canary is actually changing the distribution.

[04:41] Paula Mendes: For v1, I want the Console to show a clear error: “Cannot start experiment while route has an active canary rollout.” So functionally the precedence is moot for normal flows.

[04:54] Jada Williams: Okay, but we still need runtime behavior for the case of config drift. I’d propose: if both present, do not run experiment and emit an audit warning. That keeps safety and prevents silent weirdness.

[05:09] Sean Gallagher: +1. Also, that should be an alert for internal, because it means control-plane validation failed or someone used an API.

[05:19] Dylan Brooks: Great. So: validation blocks overlap; runtime: canary wins, experiment suppressed, and we emit a structured event/audit log.

[05:31] Jordan Lee: I’ll write that into the precedence proposal. We should be careful that “suppressed” doesn’t break clients. It just behaves like no experiment.

[05:40] Caleb Johnson: From telemetry, we should not emit exposure events if experiment suppressed, otherwise dashboards show phantom exposures.

[05:50] Logan Wright: Exactly. Okay, shifting to exposure logging.

[05:56] Logan Wright: We need to decide what constitutes an exposure. Is it “request got assigned to variant” or “request was actually served by variant’s primary target.” With fallbacks, those differ.

[06:11] Nadia Rahman: And from cost attribution, the cost is based on what actually ran, so we’ll need final served model + variant label, and ideally a routing path field.

[06:25] Marcus Lin: Security/privacy: we need to treat exposure logs as sensitive. We cannot log raw prompts. We should avoid raw user IDs unless it’s a Redwood-generated stable id. Customer-provided headers are risky.

[06:40] Jordan Lee: Current draft says hash inputs can be tenant_id + route_id + api_key_id + maybe user_id header if present. The hash is one-way, but if user_id is email, that’s PII even if hashed? It’s debatable.

[06:56] Marcus Lin: It’s still derived from PII, and depending on jurisdiction it can count. Better: allow a “redwood-sticky-id” header that customers populate with a random identifier, and we document: don’t send emails.

[07:12] Mina Haddad: But in practice customers will send whatever. We need guardrails: maybe we only accept a specific header name and we never store it, we just hash it in-memory.

[07:27] Caleb Johnson: Even if we don’t store it, it flows through logs sometimes. We have to be careful gateway debug logs don’t print headers.

[07:38] Dylan Brooks: Good call. Let’s keep it: hash inputs are known safe fields. Add optional customer-provided “sticky key” only if it is explicitly enabled and we have docs.

[07:52] Paula Mendes: Product can make that an advanced toggle: “Enable custom stickiness key.” And we can warn: do not use PII.

[08:01] Sana Farid: On the stats side, stable assignment matters more than the exact key. But we also need to know if assignment changes mid-experiment, it destroys independence.

[08:14] Jordan Lee: Stickiness duration: I was thinking “forever” as long as experiment is active, based on hashing. No server-side storage needed.

[08:23] Mina Haddad: Unless the hash input changes. Like api_key rotation, or user_id missing on some requests.

[08:33] Jada Williams: We should define a priority order: use (1) explicit sticky header, else (2) api_key_id, else (3) tenant_id. If you end up on tenant_id, then it’s not really A/B, it’s tenant-level split.

[08:48] Logan Wright: But tenant-level split is acceptable for some workloads. The Console can show a warning like “Low granularity assignment key; results may be biased.”

[09:01] Dylan Brooks: Okay. Now: when do we emit exposure events?

[09:07] Caleb Johnson: If we emit at request start, we’ll count exposures even if request fails before hitting model, like auth errors.

[09:16] Mina Haddad: If we emit after first token, then TTFT metrics get weird, and we miss non-streaming requests that error before token.

[09:28] Ravi Menon: There’s a common practice: emit “assignment” at routing decision, then emit “served” on completion with final model + error code. But that’s two events per request.

[09:42] Logan Wright: Two events doubles volume. We’re already worried about volume. Also, the ingestion pipeline would need to correlate.

[09:50] Nadia Rahman: For cost we already have an end-of-request accounting event, right? If we can just add experiment_id + variant_id to that, maybe we only need one extra event.

[10:03] Caleb Johnson: Today cost/metering attaches to request_id in the gateway. We could attach experiment_id and variant_id to the existing metrics spans, and then exposure can be derived. But the “exposure log” for audit is still needed.

[10:21] Marcus Lin: Audit wants a record that the experiment was actually applied. Aggregated metrics are not enough. But we could store a sampled log.

[10:32] Allison Grant: Sampling is key. We don’t need 100% exposures in logs to compute p95 latency; metrics already do that.

[10:41] Logan Wright: Proposal: metrics get experiment_id and variant_id labels at 100% (but very low cardinality). Exposure logs are sampled, e.g. 1% or dynamic based on QPS. Exposure logs used for debugging and audit trail.

[10:58] Sean Gallagher: Careful: metrics cardinality with experiment_id could be high if customers create lots of experiments. Need a limit. Like only active experiments, and tag as “experiment_hash” maybe.

[11:11] Allison Grant: We can enforce: at most N active experiments per org, and at most M experiments per route. And tags should be fixed length, not free-form names.

[11:25] Paula Mendes: That’s in scope for validation. We can cap active experiments.

[11:31] Jada Williams: The event schema should include: experiment_id, variant_id, route_id, project_id, org_id, region, timestamp, assignment_key_type (api_key, sticky_header, tenant), and a boolean “suppressed.” Also final served model maybe as a separate field.

[11:50] Logan Wright: That’s already a lot. Need to confirm which are required. Route_id and experiment_id are must. Org and project are needed for filtering in Console.

[12:02] Mei Lin: For reporting dataset, we’ll likely aggregate by experiment_id + variant_id + time bucket + region. We do not want route_id in the fact table at high volume. But we can include route_id in a dimension table.

[12:18] Dylan Brooks: Mei, can you propose that shape and how it feeds the Console query API? It’s a dependency.

[12:25] Mei Lin: Yep.

[12:28] Olivia Grant: Quick note on eval harness: offline eval results will have experiment_id and variant mapping. That’s a separate pipeline. We’ll need consistent variant IDs.

[12:39] Sana Farid: Also need to show confidence intervals. But please, no p-values in v1 UI, or if we do, we need explanation copy. But that’s more for Design.

[12:51] Dylan Brooks: Back to telemetry pipeline changes. Caleb, what’s the concern?

[12:56] Caleb Johnson: Ingest pipeline: if we add new tags to gateway metrics, we need schema versioning and allowlists. Also, we need to keep the tag set consistent across latency metrics, error metrics, and cost. Otherwise dashboards don’t join.

[13:13] Logan Wright: We should define “metrics schema v1”: list of required dimensions, and a hard rule: no additional dimensions without review.

[13:21] Allison Grant: +1. Also, “variant_name” should never be a dimension. Only variant_id, which is stable and short.

[13:29] Paula Mendes: But customers want names in UI.

[13:32] Allison Grant: UI can join to config DB to display names. Metrics should not.

[13:38] Nadia Rahman: Same for model names. Use model_id not full “meta-llama/whatever:sha”.

[13:45] Mina Haddad: For routing we already have internal model IDs. That’s fine.

[13:51] Ravi Menon: On the “served model” field: we can keep a small enum for “served_primary” vs “served_fallback_compat” vs “served_fallback_region.” That’s low cardinality.

[14:06] Jordan Lee: That’s good. It answers Mina’s earlier point: variant label stays constant, but we can break down within variant by served path.

[14:17] Dylan Brooks: Great. Now, deterministic assignment with retries and streaming reconnect. Mina, what’s the issue in practice?

[14:25] Mina Haddad: If a client streams, disconnects, and retries with the same request payload, our gateway sometimes generates a new request_id. If the hash input includes request_id, assignment flips. We should not include request_id.

[14:40] Jordan Lee: Agree. Hash inputs should be stable across retries. We should use api_key_id and route_id and maybe a client-provided idempotency key.

[14:51] Jada Williams: We can also treat idempotency_key as highest priority if present. That gives stable assignment per logical request.

[15:00] Marcus Lin: Careful with idempotency key if it contains PII. But typically it’s random.

[15:08] Caleb Johnson: Gateway already has Idempotency-Key header support on some endpoints. We can reuse it.

[15:17] Dylan Brooks: Decision: do not use request_id. Prefer idempotency key if present; else api_key_id; else tenant_id fallback with warning.

[15:27] Paula Mendes: And we need to document that if you want per-user assignment, you should provide a non-PII sticky key.

[15:34] Logan Wright: Now, sampling: do we sample exposure logs at gateway or in pipeline?

[15:41] Caleb Johnson: Gateway sampling is cheaper. But we need deterministic sampling maybe, so the sample is unbiased across variants.

[15:50] Sana Farid: For debugging it doesn’t matter. For using sampled logs for any analytics, it matters. But we said we won’t use exposure logs for aggregate stats.

[16:01] Logan Wright: Exactly. Aggregates come from metrics, not exposure logs. So simple random sampling in gateway is fine.

[16:10] Sean Gallagher: But if exposure logs are used for incident debugging, we need enough coverage. If we sample at 1% and customer is low QPS, it’s useless.

[16:20] Logan Wright: We can do adaptive sampling: min 50 events per hour per experiment, cap at e.g. 1%. Something like that.

[16:31] Allison Grant: Adaptive sampling itself can be complex. Maybe keep it simple: default 5% during beta, then reduce later. Or per-tier.

[16:42] Dylan Brooks: Let’s do: fixed default for beta (say 5%), and design in a knob for adaptive later. ADR-0188 can mention it as future.

[16:52] Marcus Lin: Retention: exposure logs retention should be shorter. Maybe 7-14 days. Aggregated metrics can be longer.

[17:01] Paula Mendes: Beta customers will want at least 30 days of results.

[17:05] Mei Lin: Aggregates in the reporting dataset can be stored 30-90 days depending on plan. Raw logs short.

[17:14] Dylan Brooks: Okay.

[17:16] Dylan Brooks: Let’s touch on privacy constraints explicitly for ADR-0188.

[17:22] Marcus Lin: Constraints: no raw prompts, no response bodies, no full headers dump, no IP address in exposure event by default. Org/project IDs are okay. api_key_id might be sensitive but internal.

[17:35] Logan Wright: We need “api_key_id” only if it’s used for assignment debug. But we can store “assignment_key_type” and “assignment_key_hash” instead.

[17:45] Jordan Lee: That’s better. We can store a short hash of the key to correlate without storing the original.

[17:52] Caleb Johnson: But hashing a key for each request adds CPU. Not huge, but at gateway scale it matters.

[18:00] Mina Haddad: We’re already hashing for bucketing. We can reuse the hash output. Like store “bucket_hash” or “assignment_hash” truncated.

[18:10] Logan Wright: Great, and that also avoids double hashing.

[18:14] Dylan Brooks: Nice. So exposure event includes assignment_hash (truncated), not raw key.

[18:22] Nadia Rahman: One more: billing. Adding experiment_id to cost attribution must not change the billing numbers. It’s a dimension for analysis only.

[18:33] Dylan Brooks: Yes. We should confirm with billing pipeline owners.

[18:37] Nadia Rahman: I’ll check. I suspect we need to ensure it doesn’t change aggregation keys upstream.

[18:45] Allison Grant: On dashboards: experiment_id as a template variable, graphs show A vs B, plus guardrail panels. We need to wire guardrail evaluator to alerts.

[18:58] Sean Gallagher: Which brings guardrails: what metrics do we guard? At minimum error rate and latency regression. Also 429 rate.

[19:07] Paula Mendes: The PRD says max allowed p95 latency regression and error thresholds. We need numbers.

[19:14] Sean Gallagher: For beta, I propose: p95 end-to-end latency +15% over baseline for 10 minutes triggers warning; +25% for 5 minutes triggers auto rollback. Error rate: +1% absolute or +50% relative, whichever smaller. And 429s should be separate.

[19:34] Allison Grant: We also need to define baseline: variant A is control. But what if variant A is not stable due to traffic? That’s tricky.

[19:44] Sana Farid: Statistically, doing automated rollback based on short windows is noisy. But SRE wants safety. Keep it conservative and require minimum exposure count.

[19:56] Sean Gallagher: Right. Rollback triggers only if there are at least X requests in window, say 500. Otherwise alert-only.

[20:07] Dylan Brooks: Let’s capture that. Sean, can you send requirements in email / doc? We’ll put them into the SLO/guardrail policy.

[20:18] Sean Gallagher: Yup.

[20:20] Jada Williams: Another question: if experiment causes problems, do we rollback to 100% control, or disable experiment entirely? I think disable.

[20:28] Ravi Menon: Disable experiment. But also we should preserve config for audit and allow restart.

[20:35] Paula Mendes: Console flow: Stop experiment, status becomes “Stopped,” traffic returns to previous pinned model. Rollback is a separate action that also reverts route config changes.

[20:48] Dylan Brooks: Okay.

[20:50] Dylan Brooks: Back to precedence again quickly: where do fallback policies sit? Mina?

[20:55] Mina Haddad: Fallback must always be allowed after a model selection, because that’s reliability. So: experiment chooses variant -> variant chooses target model -> request executes -> fallback may happen. But we should not re-run assignment after fallback.

[21:12] Jordan Lee: Exactly. And in the event we fallback to a different model, we still keep experiment_id and variant_id. And add served_path.

[21:22] Logan Wright: Then reporting can show “variant B had 20% fallback served,” which explains latency.

[21:29] Dylan Brooks: Great.

[21:31] Caleb Johnson: Pipeline note: adding served_path might require updating the metrics aggregator. But it’s low cardinality so OK.

[21:41] Allison Grant: As long as served_path has like 3-5 values. Not free text.

[21:46] Logan Wright: We’ll define the enum.

[21:49] Dylan Brooks: Let’s talk about schema versioning.

[21:52] Caleb Johnson: We should include schema_version in exposure events. For metrics, we can version the dashboards and the allowlist config. But metrics systems don’t love versions.

[22:02] Logan Wright: Exposure event: schema_version = 1. Metrics schema: in docs. If we must add something later, we do additive, and keep old dashboards working.

[22:13] Mei Lin: For the reporting dataset, I’d like to store schema_version as a column for safety. But we can default to 1.

[22:22] Dylan Brooks: Okay.

[22:24] Olivia Grant: Small thing: variant_id format. If we use UUID, it’s fine. But for logs/metrics, long IDs can be heavy. We might use short IDs.

[22:36] Logan Wright: We can use ULID or a short base32 token. Or we can have internal numeric IDs. But that’s a bigger change.

[22:45] Jada Williams: For v1, we can keep UUID in config store, but emit a shortened hash for metrics tags. Like variant_tag = first 8 chars.

[22:56] Allison Grant: Please no truncating without collision handling. But 8 chars of UUID is probably okay? Still risky.

[23:04] Jordan Lee: Safer: generate a dedicated “variant_tag” that is unique per experiment, like A, B, C, plus an experiment_tag. But then you need experiment context.

[23:14] Logan Wright: Actually that’s good: variant_tag can be “control” and “treatment” for two-variant case. But we said UI confusion. Also, customers can have >2 variants.

[23:25] Paula Mendes: In UI we can call them “Variant 1/2” and let them name them.

[23:30] Dylan Brooks: For metrics tags, we can do: experiment_id short hash (like 10 chars) + variant_index small int. That’s low cardinality and short.

[23:41] Mei Lin: Works for dataset joins as long as we can map back in config.

[23:46] Marcus Lin: And short hashes still count as identifiers; access control still required.

[23:52] Dylan Brooks: Yep.

[23:54] Logan Wright: Okay, let’s capture: metrics tags use experiment_tag (generated) and variant_index. Exposure log can store full experiment_id for audit, but that log is access controlled.

[24:10] Caleb Johnson: That’s doable.

[24:12] Dylan Brooks: Great. Any other pipeline concerns?

[24:16] Caleb Johnson: Cardinality checks in CI. Like before we merge PRs that add tags, we run a static check or review. We can have an allowlist file.

[24:26] Allison Grant: Already doing that for some metrics. We can extend.

[24:31] Dylan Brooks: Good.

[24:33] Sana Farid: Quick: results reporting needs to indicate minimum sample. If people run 90/10 and only have 50 requests in B, they’ll overinterpret.

[24:44] Paula Mendes: Design is adding “Insufficient data” states.

[24:48] Dylan Brooks: Okay.

[24:50] Dylan Brooks: Let’s do a round on open questions we haven’t resolved.

[24:55] Mina Haddad: One: How do we handle retries without idempotency key? If client retries, and assignment is based on api_key_id, then it’s stable. So fine.

[25:05] Jordan Lee: Unless they use multiple keys. But that’s not solvable.

[25:10] Logan Wright: Another: Should exposure logs include request_id for debugging? That can be high-cardinality but in logs it’s fine.

[25:19] Marcus Lin: Request_id is okay if it’s internal and not correlatable outside. But it can be used to join to other logs. We need access control.

[25:29] Sean Gallagher: For incident response, request_id is useful. But again, sampled logs might miss the bad request.

[25:36] Logan Wright: We can include request_id only in sampled exposure logs, not in metrics.

[25:42] Caleb Johnson: That’s fine.

[25:44] Mei Lin: For dataset, we don’t need request_id.

[25:47] Dylan Brooks: Good.

[25:49] Paula Mendes: Another open one: Dedicated and Private. Hosted and Dedicated must work. Private maybe follow-on. Does anything in telemetry design assume hosted infra?

[26:02] Caleb Johnson: Exposure logging from gateway exists in hosted and dedicated. Private can run the gateway but may not have our central pipeline. So we need a mode where logs are local.

[26:12] Marcus Lin: That’s why we should gate Private. Also compliance questions.

[26:18] Dylan Brooks: Cool. We’ll state “Private not supported in beta” in PRD.

[26:24] Allison Grant: Another question: do we need per-region splits or just global? The PRD says eligibility rules like region.

[26:33] Ravi Menon: We can scope experiments by region, but assignment should include region in hash so it’s stable per region. But then a user traveling region changes variant.

[26:45] Sana Farid: That’s okay; region is effectively a different experiment population.

[26:50] Jordan Lee: If region is part of assignment inputs, it changes assignment. But is that desired? If experiment is configured only in eu-west, then other regions shouldn’t be in experiment anyway.

[27:02] Mina Haddad: The routing layer will only evaluate experiment policy if region eligible. So region doesn't need to be in the hash for those ineligible.

[27:11] Dylan Brooks: So: region used as eligibility filter, not necessarily as hash input, unless we want within-region independence.

[27:20] Logan Wright: For reporting, we want breakdown by region. But that’s just a dimension in metrics, not hash input.

[27:28] Dylan Brooks: Great.

[27:30] Dylan Brooks: Let’s do quick recap of decisions.

[27:34] Dylan Brooks: One: Experiments and canaries are mutually exclusive on same route (v1). Validation blocks start. Runtime precedence: canary wins; experiment suppressed; emit audit/warning event.

[27:48] Dylan Brooks: Two: Assignment hash inputs: do not use request_id. Priority: idempotency key if present, else optional customer sticky key (explicitly enabled), else api_key_id, else tenant_id with warning.

[28:03] Dylan Brooks: Three: Exposure logging: metrics dimensions at 100% include experiment_tag + variant_index and minimal other dims; sampled exposure logs include full experiment_id and request_id, plus assignment_hash and served_path enum. No PII.

[28:19] Dylan Brooks: Four: served_path enum to indicate fallback vs primary, to interpret performance.

[28:26] Dylan Brooks: Five: schema versioning on exposure events; strict allowlist for metrics tags; cardinality review.

[28:34] Dylan Brooks: Six: retention: raw exposure logs short (TBD, likely 14 days), aggregates longer (30+ days depending on plan).

[28:44] Dylan Brooks: Guardrails: Sean to propose thresholds and min sample before auto rollback.

[28:51] Dylan Brooks: Did I miss anything?

[28:54] Jada Williams: We should also note that exposure logs are not the source of truth for stats; metrics are. That matters for sampling.

[29:01] Logan Wright: Yep.

[29:03] Dylan Brooks: Cool.

[29:05] (crosstalk)

[29:06] Allison Grant: One more nit: experiment_tag generation. Needs to be stable and unique. Don’t let customers set it.

[29:12] Jordan Lee: We can generate from experiment_id and store it.

[29:16] Dylan Brooks: Great.

[29:18] Dylan Brooks: Remaining time, let’s capture open questions for ADR text.

[29:23] Jordan Lee: Open: what’s the default sampling rate for beta? Dylan said 5%. Confirm with SRE.

[29:31] Sean Gallagher: 5% is probably okay. But we should cap absolute volume too. If someone runs 50k QPS, 5% is too big.

[29:40] Logan Wright: Good point. Maybe “min(5%, 200 events/sec)” or something.

[29:48] Caleb Johnson: Implementing a per-second cap in gateway is feasible.

[29:53] Dylan Brooks: Let’s mark as open: sampling policy includes cap.
